neutral_facts.value: The accused borrowed a total of Rs. 64,000 from the complainant and issued three cheques, two of which were returned by the bank as dishonoured. The complainant received an intimation from the bank about the dishonour of the cheques on 08.04.1991. The complainant issued a legal notice to the accused on 12.04.1991, which was returned with a postal endorsement indicating the addressee was absent. The complainant sent another legal notice on 04.05.1991, which was returned with a postal endorsement indicating it was refused. The complainant then filed a complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The Trial Court convicted the accused, and the Appellate Court upheld the conviction. The High Court reversed the conviction, arguing that the second notice was sent beyond the 15-day limit. The Supreme Court overturned the High Court's decision, finding that the first notice was valid and the second notice was merely a reminder.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the first respondent failed to return the borrowed amount Rs. 64,000/- for which statutory notice under proviso (b) of Section 138 of the N.I. Act was issued to him to make good the dishonoured cheques due to insufficiency of funds in his bank account. The appellant lodged a private complaint before the Judicial First Class Magistrate-II, Alappuzha for the alleged offence under Section 138 of the N.I. Act.

quotes.text: The prosecution argued that the first respondent failed to return the borrowed amount Rs. 64,000/- for which statutory notice under proviso (b) of Section 13,8 of the N.I. defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the provisions of Section 138 of the N.I. Act cannot be invoked as the appellant had not complied with the conditions in Clause (b) of the proviso to the said section. Notice demanding payment of the amount arising from the two dishonoured cheques in question was on 04-05-1991, whereas the intimation regarding dishonour of the said cheques was given by the appellant's bank on 08-04-1991. Therefore, the notice was beyond 15 days.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that once notice is sent by registered post by correctly addressing to the drawer of the cheque, the service of notice is deemed to have been effected. The Court also emphasized that the object of providing Clause (c) of Section 138 is to avoid unnecessary hardship and that the right of an honest lender cannot be defeated.

quotes.text: Once notice is sent by registered post by correctly addressing to the drawer of the cheque, the service of notice is deemed to have been effected.
The right of an honest lender cannot be defeated as has happened in this case.
